To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of group discussions are dependent on societal‐level factors and that polarization processes between local groups within the same social category are predicted by the perceived local group norm.
group discussions can lead to polarization between majority sub‐groups, especially when the societal context is characterized by a negative norm regarding a minority group.
group discussions can polarize people's attitudes towards a minority category in a negative norm context, but only if the group norm is perceived as positive.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the societal‐level context affects group processes.
the question of how the societal context affects intergroup relations.
the development of inter‐group attitudes in a negative societal normative context, and how this development can be influenced by group discussions in a local context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the polarization effects of group discussion were found to be stronger in the negative norm condition than in the positive norm condition.
the negative societal norm about a minority can fuel polarization between local groups at the local level, but only when the groups discuss the ambiguous behaviour of a minority member.
group discussions are a double‐edged sword, as they have the potential to both promote and reduce polarization, depending on societal context and group processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the polarization of groups within a broader category is a function of the interaction between the local group context and the societal context, and this polarization is predicted by the a‐priori perceived norm of the local group.
societal level factors can influence the local group discussion and this discussion in turn can lead to a polarized view of a minority group member.
the polarization of groups within a broader category is a function of the societal context in which these groups operate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
societal change can be studied by combining societal‐, group, and individual‐ level factors.
group discussions in a negative norm can polarize between majority subgroups.
the societal context can fuel local polarization processes, and these effects are mediated by group discussions.
